explanation: Verbs such as studieren (to study) and reparieren (to repair) form their past participle without ge-. Only -t is added to the stem.
example: studieren -> studiert,  reparieren -> repariert

rule: Separable verbs (not ending in ieren) can form their past participle with -ge- and -en.
explanation: Separable verbs (not ending in ieren) can form their past participle with -ge- and -en.
example: Sie ist früh eingeschlafen. (She fell asleep early.)

rule: Past participle separable verbs ending in -ieren
explanation: Verbs ending in -ieren form their past participle without ge-. Only the -t is added to the stem. The past participles of these verbs  always end in -t.
example: Wir haben den Traktor repariert. (We fixed the tractor.)

explanation: In German, the superlative is primarily formed by adding -(e)st to the adjective and placing am before it (meaning "at the most"). The exact construction depends on whether you are using the adjective in a sentence as a description or right before a noun.
example:
1. The Standard Rule (Predicative/Adverbial)
When the adjective describes a verb or comes after the noun, you use the formula: am + adjective stem + -sten.

schnell (fast) -> am schnellsten (fastest)
billig (cheap) -> am billigsten (cheapest)

2. Pronunciation Rule
If the adjective ends in a -d, -t, -s, -ß, -sch, -x, or -z, insert an extra -e- before the -sten for easier pronunciation.

alt (old) -> am ältesten (oldest)
süß (sweet) -> am süßesten (sweetest)

3. Vowel Changes (Umlauts) Many common, short (one-syllable) adjectives with a, o, or u as the root vowel will get an umlaut (ä, ö, ü) in the superlative.

groß (big) -> am größten (biggest)
jung (young) -> am jüngsten (youngest)

4. Attributive Form (Before a Noun) If the superlative adjective is modifying a noun directly (e.g., "the biggest house"), it does not use "am". Instead, it uses the definite article (der/die/das) + adjective stem + -(e)ste + adjective endings based on the case.

Das ist das größte Haus. (This is the biggest house.)
Sie ist die netteste Frau. (She is the nicest woman.)

5. Irregular Superlatives/  A few common adjectives change their root entirely and must be memorized:
gut (good) -> am besten (best)
viel (much) ->am meisten (most)
gern (gladly) -> am liebsten (most gladly)

explanation:
As in English, you use the Passiv (passive voice) in German if you don't know who performed an action or whoever performed it is irrelevant.

The Passiv is often used in general or universal statements and can be formed in every tense.

The Passiv is formed with a form of werden and the past participle.  The past participle is always at the end of the sentence.
example:
Die Firma wurde im Jahr 1900 gegründet.   The company was founded in 1900.

Der Blinde wird geführt.  The blind (man) is being guided.

In Deutschland werden viele Autos produziert.   In Germany, lots of cars are produced.

explanation:
These conjunctions connect two independent main clauses. They sit in "Position 0" (between the clauses) and do not affect the normal subject-verb word order.

Common words: und (and), aber (but), oder (or), denn (because), sondern (but rather).

Structure: [Main Clause 1] + [Conjunction] + [Main Clause 2]
example: Ich gehe einkaufen, und mein Bruder kocht das Abendessen. (I go shopping, and my brother cooks dinner.)

explanation:
These connect a main clause to a dependent clause. The subordinating conjunction introduces the dependent clause and forces the conjugated verb to the very end of that clause.

Common words: weil (because), dass (that), wenn (if/when), obwohl (although), bevor (before).Structure: [Main Clause], + [Conjunction] + [Subject] + ... + [Verb]
example: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil es regnet. (I stay at home because it is raining.)

explanation:
These are paired connectors that coordinate or subordinate two elements together. They are placed exactly before the elements or clauses they are comparing.

Common words: entweder ... oder (either ... or), weder ... noch (neither ... nor), sowohl ... als auch (both ... and), je ... desto (the ... the).

Structure: [Part 1] [First clause/item], + [Part 2] [Second clause/item]
example: Ich möchte entweder Kaffee oder Tee. (I would like either coffee or tea.)

explanation:
dependent clauses use the SOV (Subject-Object-Verb) structure.Standard Dependent Clause StructureThe Trigger: 
1. Starts with a subordinating conjunction (e.g., weil (because), dass (that), obwohl (although), wenn (if)) or a relative pronoun (e.g., der, die, das).
2, The Subject: Appears right after the conjunction.
3.The Middle: Objects, adverbs, and negated words (like nicht) fill the space in the middle.
4. The End: The conjugated verb is placed at the absolute end of the clause.
example: "Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin."(I am staying at home because I am sick.)

rule: Mention the person or thing by whom an action is performed (i.e. the agent)
explanation: If you want to mention the person or thing by whom an action is performed (i.e. the agent), you can use von followed by the dative.
example:
Grace wird von einem Freund durch die Stadt geführt. ( Grace is being guided through the town by a friend.)

Die Nationalhymne wurde von Haydn komponiert, nicht von Mozart. (The national anthem was composed by Haydn, not by Mozart.)

rule: To mention an agent that isn't a living thing by whom an action is performed
explanation: It is expressed with durch plus accusative, e.g. Das Haus wurde durch den Sturm zerstört. (The house was destroyed by the storm.)

A relative clause describes a person or thing more precisely. It always refers to someone or something (noun) already mentioned in the sentence.

German relative pronounds are der, die, das.

Relative clauses start with a relative pronoun. The relative pronoun refers to a previous noun and agrees in gender and number.

In relative clauses, the verb comes at the end
example:
Das ist der Junge, der brav ist. -That's the boy who's well-behaved.

Die Frau, die dort steht, ist seine Mutter. - The woman who is standing over there is his mother.

explanation:
As a relative pronoun does not necessarily have to be a subject, it does not always stay in the nominative.

All forms are the same as the articles except for the plural form in the dative, which is denen.
example:
Das ist mein Kollege, den ich gern mag. (That is my colleague, who I like.  Mögen uses the accusative.)

Die Frau, der ich das Geschenk gab, war meine Freundin. (The woman who I gave the present to was my friend.  Geben uses the dative)

Das sind die Eltern, mit denen ich einen Streit hatte. (Those are the parents with whom I had an argument.     denen - plural form in dative)

explanation:
Use als for unequal comparisons (meaning "than"). It is used alongside comparative adjectives (ending in "-er").

Use wie for equal comparisons (meaning "as") or similarities (meaning "like"). It is used with the base (unmodified) form of adjectives.
example:
1. Als: Comparisons of Difference ("Than")
Use als when comparing two things that are not equal. It translates directly to the English word "than".

Structure: [Comparative Adjective] + als

Example: Mein Auto ist schneller als dein Auto. (My car is faster than your car.)
Example: Er ist größer als sein Vater. (He is taller than his father.)

2. Wie: Comparisons of Equality ("As ... As")
Use wie when two things or people are the same, equal, or share a similarity. It typically translates to "as" or "like".

Structure: so + [Base Adjective] + wie

Example: Er ist so groß wie sein Vater. (He is as tall as his father.)
Example: Sie singt wie ein Engel. (She sings like an angel.)

rule: Accusative case personal and reflexive pronouns
explanation:
Accusative case (direct object) indicating a person or thing, words ending in --self (myself, yourself,...)

ich           mich             wir      uns
du            dich              ihr      euch
er/sie/es  sich              sie       sich
example:
Use the accusative when the reflexive pronoun is the only object in the sentence.

Its specific function depends on the context:

Direct Object: Used when you are receiving the action of a verb (e.g., Er sieht mich - "He sees me").

Reflexive Pronoun: Used when the subject and object are the same person (e.g., Ich wasche mich - "I wash myself" / "I am washing" ).

With Prepositions: Used after prepositions that require the accusative case, such as für (for) or ohne (without) (e.g., ohne mich - "without me").

explanation: German personal pronouns (Personalpronomen) replace nouns and refer to people or things. They change form depending on whether they are the subject (Nominative), the direct object (Accusative), or the indirect object (Dative). Note that in German, you must distinguish between formal and informal forms of "you".
example:
Nominative       Accusative          Dative            
                    (Subject)         (Direct Object)    (Indirect Object)
 
I/me                   ich                    mich                mir
You(informal)    du                     dich                 dir
He/Him               er                     ihn                   ihm
She/He               sie                    sie                   ihr
It                         es                     es                    ihm
We/Us                wir                    uns                  uns
You(informal)    ihr                     euch                euch
They/Them        sie                     sie                   ihnen
Formal               Sie                     Sie                   Ihnen

How the Forms Work in Sentences
1. Nominative (The Subject)
Used when the pronoun is doing the action.
Ich (I) kenne den Mann. (I know the man.)

2. Accusative (The Direct Object)
Used when the pronoun is directly receiving the action.
Der Mann sieht mich. (The man sees me.)

3. Dative (The Indirect Object)
Used when the pronoun is the recipient (answering "to whom?").
Er gibt mir das Buch. (He gives the book to me.)

explanation:
German possessive pronouns replace a noun entirely (e.g., "mine" instead of "my car"). They must match the replaced noun's possessor, gender, number, and sentence case (Nominative, Accusative, Dative, or Genitive). 

Possessive pronouns are used to indicate possession of non-people! They are the very last or very first word in a sentence.
example:
Mine                        mein-               Our     unser-
Yours(informal)      dein-                Your (informal, plural)   euer-, eur-
His/Its                     sein-                 Their(plural, formal)      ihr-
Her's                       ihr-

example:
das Foto -> die Fotos
das Büro -> die Büros

explanation: Plural form takes no ending
example: der Fehler -> die Fehler

explanation: Plural forms take -en
example: die Besprechung -> die Besprechungen

explanation: Plural form usually take -n
example: die Blume -> die Blumen

explanation:
You only need to add endings to German adjectives when they appear immediately before the noun they modify. If the adjective is used after a linking verb (predicate position), it remains unchanged.

1. The Adjective is After the Noun (Predicate Adjective)
If the adjective follows a verb (like sein - to be), it takes no ending.
Der Hund ist groß. (The dog is big.)
Die Katze ist klein. (The cat is small.)

2. The Adjective is Before the Noun (Attributive Adjective)
Proper adjective ending depends on 
- the gender of the noun being modified
- the case of the noun being modified
- which declension pattern (<– there are 4) is being used

Adjectives take an -en ending in all other cases, as well as for all plural nouns.
Example: Der rote Ball (The red ball - nominative) vs. Ich sehe den roten Ball

When preceded by an Indefinite Article (ein, eine) or Possessive Word (mein, dein):


Adjectives borrow the ending of the definite article to clearly show the gender of the noun.
Example (Nominative): Ein großer Hund (A big dog - masculine), 
Ein kleines Kind (A small child - neuter)
Eine schöne Blume (A beautiful flower - feminine). 

When there is No Article (Zero Article):
The adjective must do the heavy lifting to signal the noun's gender and case, so it takes "strong" endings.

Example: Ich trinke kaltes Wasser (I drink cold water).

Noch einmal ... - Once again
Dieses mal ... - This time

example:

verb + gern

explanation: Use kein to negate nouns without an article or with an indefinite article, and use nicht to negate verbs, adjectives, adverbs, and nouns with definite articles. Think of kein as meaning "not a" or "no/not any," while nicht acts as a standalone "not".
example:
When to use kein
Use it for nouns to express absence or non-existence.
It replaces the indefinite article (ein/eine).
Because it functions like an article, it must match the noun's gender, case, and number (e.g., kein, keine, keinen).

Example: Ich habe kein Auto. (I have no car / I do not have a car).
Example: Er trinkt keine Milch. (He drinks no milk).


When to use nicht
Use it for verbs, adjectives, adverbs, and nouns with a definite article.
It never changes form.
Example (Verb): Ich schwimme nicht. (I do not swim).
Example (Adjective): Das Haus ist nicht groß. (The house is not big).
Example (Definite noun): Ich mag nicht den Film. (I do not like the movie).

explanation:
Both words mean "because" or "since," but they differ grammatically and stylistically. 

Weil introduces a subordinate clause, pushing the conjugated verb to the end. 

Denn links two main clauses, keeping the normal subject-verb word order, and cannot begin a sentence.
example:
Ich bleibe heute zu Hause, weil ich müde bin.

Ich bleibe heute zu Hause, denn ich bin müde.
